identification.summary: CrowdStrike tracks CIRCUS SPIDER as the Russian-speaking criminal actor that develops and maintains the NetWalker ransomware (also called Mailto) [S1][S2]. NetWalker was first discovered in September 2019 with a compilation timestamp of 28 August 2019, and was used in big game hunting style operations and spam distribution [S1]. Unit 42 dates the move to a ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) model to March 2020, with the CIRCUS SPIDER group recruiting affiliates [S2].
identification.firstObserved: Malware first discovered September 2019; compilation timestamp 28 August 2019 [S1].
identification.notes: CIRCUS SPIDER is CrowdStrike's actor name; NetWalker/Mailto is the malware family. Some third-party coverage describes it as part of a larger syndicate (Comparitech, naming MUMMY SPIDER); this was seen only in a search summary and is not adopted here. No Microsoft actor name was identified in the sources gathered. Names of malware (Mailto, Kazakavkovkiz per a search summary of ACSC) are not added as actor aliases.

attribution.sponsor: Financially motivated Russian-speaking criminal group; no state sponsor is stated in the sources gathered [S1][S2].
attribution.confidence: CrowdStrike's attribution of NetWalker development to CIRCUS SPIDER is a vendor assessment [S1]. Law enforcement action in 2021 targeted infrastructure and one affiliate, not the core developers [S4][S6].
attribution.basis: CrowdStrike technical analysis of NetWalker (CSIT-20081, June 2020) [S1]; Unit 42 ransomware threat assessment describing the RaaS recruitment and requirements (Russian-language ability) [S2]; affiliate recruitment posts reported by Advanced Intelligence via Threatpost [S3].

objectives: Financial gain through ransomware extortion, scaled by recruiting affiliates for a share of ransom payments [S2][S3].

targeting.notes: Unit 42 reports victims included hospitals, educational institutions and local governments, and COVID-19 themed phishing was used against hospitals [S2]. DOJ stated attacks specifically targeted healthcare during the COVID-19 pandemic [S4][S6]. Affiliates were asked to go after larger, higher-paying targets [S2].

capabilities.summary: NetWalker ransomware with a closed affiliate program: CIRCUS SPIDER vets applicants, requiring proof of prior ransomware revenue, experience and intended industry [S1]. Unit 42 lists affiliate requirements including Russian-language ability, red team experience and proof of prior experience [S2]. Reported revenue split was 20 percent to operators and 80 percent to affiliates per Advanced Intelligence [S3]. Distribution included spam and COVID-19 lures as well as big game hunting intrusions [S1][S2]. DOJ described a dark web resource used by affiliates to give victims payment instructions [S4].

campaigns.name: NetWalker (Mailto) first observed
campaigns.summary: NetWalker discovered, compile timestamp 28 August 2019; used in big game hunting and spam distribution [S1].

campaigns.name: Shift to RaaS and affiliate recruitment
campaigns.summary: CIRCUS SPIDER moves NetWalker to a RaaS model and recruits experienced affiliates; reported 80/20 affiliate split [S2][S3].

campaigns.name: COVID-19 themed healthcare targeting
campaigns.summary: COVID-19 themed phishing used against hospitals and a medical research university by groups using NetWalker [S2]. CrowdStrike noted COVID-19 lures and healthcare targeting suggested pandemic exploitation [S1].

campaigns.name: US-Bulgarian disruption and affiliate charged
campaigns.summary: DOJ announced action with Bulgarian authorities: a dark web resource used by affiliates was seized, about $454,530 in cryptocurrency seized, and Canadian affiliate Sebastien Vachon-Desjardins charged; he was arrested in Canada [S4][S6].

campaigns.name: Affiliate sentenced
campaigns.summary: Vachon-Desjardins sentenced to 20 years in Tampa federal court after guilty pleas and ordered to forfeit 21.5 million USD [S6].

diamond.adversary: Russian-speaking criminal developer group (CIRCUS SPIDER) plus vetted affiliates, at least one of whom was a Canadian national [S1][S2][S6].
diamond.capability: NetWalker ransomware, spam and COVID-19 phishing delivery, big game hunting intrusions by affiliates [S1][S2].
diamond.infrastructure: Dark web victim payment resource, seized by Bulgarian authorities in January 2021 [S4]; cryptocurrency payments [S4].
diamond.victim: Hospitals, schools, local governments and private firms [S2].
diamond.socioPolitical: Criminal profit motive exploiting the COVID-19 pandemic; no state tasking evidenced [S1][S4].
diamond.technology: Windows enterprise environments; phishing-exposed users and healthcare networks [S2].

gaps: Primary documents were not opened: the CrowdStrike report (CSIT-20081), DOJ press releases and Unit 42 page could not be fetched (host resolution failed), so facts rely on search result summaries [S1][S2][S4][S6].
Source dates for S2 (Unit 42) and S3 (Threatpost) are approximate from search results.
Identity and location of core CIRCUS SPIDER developers are not public in the sources gathered; arrests concerned affiliates only.

Intrusion techniques (initial access, tooling, lateral movement) used by affiliates were not verified from primary technical reporting; Microsoft and Trend Micro write-ups were only seen second hand and are not cited.
Relation to other tracked names (MUMMY SPIDER syndicate claim, other vendor names) is unverified.
Status after the January 2021 disruption, and whether the developers resumed under other names, is unknown from these sources.
Reported sentence figures differ across outlets in some search results; the DOJ-reported 20 years is used [S6].

Two further secondary sources were dropped during fact-checking because their URLs could not be confirmed in search results; the victim, country and US-victim counts that rested only on one of them were removed.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Healthcare, education and local-government networks, including DoD-affiliated medical and university partners, are the terrain this actor class has hit [S2][S4]. STEP 2: Affiliates were vetted for experience and told to pursue larger, higher-paying victims, so intrusion quality may vary by affiliate while the payload is common [S1][S2]. STEP 3: Phishing and lures tied to current events, then enterprise-wide encryption and data leak extortion via Tor [S1][S2]. STEP 4: MLCOA is financially motivated ransomware against civilian health and public-sector entities supporting installations. MDCOA is an affiliate hitting a defense-related medical or contractor network during a crisis to disrupt services and leak data. Candidate indicators: crisis-themed phishing with document lures, mass file encryption notes pointing to Tor portals, and Tor-bound traffic from internal hosts [S2].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track ransomware advisories for health and public-sector partners and watch for event-themed phishing surges [S2]. (2) Authorities: this is criminal activity, so response runs through law enforcement and DC3-type channels rather than cyber operations authorities; the 2021 action was a DOJ-led effort with Bulgarian partners [S4]. (3) Mission assurance: maintain offline backups and continuity plans for medical and installation support systems since victims were hospitals [S2][S4]. (4) Coordination: share indicators with civil partners.
